claims.text: The alloy has the composition Ti33Nb28Cr11V11Ni17 in atomic percent.
The alloy was fabricated by directed energy deposition from high-purity elemental powders on a Ti6Al4V substrate.
The as-deposited alloy is a single-phase solid solution with a predominantly BCC A2 microstructure.
The as-deposited microstructure has an average grain size of approximately 3.66 micrometers.
The as-deposited alloy has a hardness of approximately 720 HV.
Laser-assisted machining will use a TiAlN plus SH-coated flat-end mill, a feed rate of 100 mm/min, a cutting depth of 0.3 mm, and a 3 mm laser-to-tool separation.
Under the specified setup, laser preheating raises the surface temperature to approximately 930 degrees Celsius and the temperature at a depth of 0.3 mm to approximately 800 degrees Celsius.
The approximately 800–930 degrees Celsius preheating condition places the alloy's near-surface layer in a softening regime.
Localized laser preheating softens the near-surface region and reduces its strength and hardness.
Near-surface softening reduces cutting resistance and cutting force.
Laser preheating limits machining-induced strain hardening, grain refinement, and mechanical damage.
Machining removes most of the laser-generated heat-affected layer.
Removal of the heat-affected layer preserves a larger grain structure in the remaining material.
Laser-assisted machining preserves the alloy's configurational entropy and solid-solution strengthening.
Compared with conventional machining, laser-assisted machining produces lower cutting forces.
Compared with conventional machining, laser-assisted machining improves surface finish and reduces work hardening.
Compared with conventional machining, laser-assisted machining retains a grain-size and hardness distribution closer to the as-deposited state.
Compared with conventional machining, laser-assisted machining improves the alloy's tensile behavior at elevated temperatures up to 1000 degrees Celsius under controlled argon conditions.
